theme: Save the call for the good part. When you already know a normal morning happened, a call across the distance can be about the bike, the chess game, or nothing at all.

posts.text: Calling a parent across time zones can turn into a quick status check. How are you, did you sleep, talk soon. Kettle tells the family a normal morning happened, so the call is free to be about something else.
posts.alt: Three-panel comic. Dana, at her table, phones her dad: 'Hi Dad. What are you building?' Walt, at his garage workbench with a bicycle brake in his hands, answers: 'A new brake. Listen to this.' Dana laughs on the call. Caption: The call got to be about the bike.

posts.title: Three ways to make a call to a parent about something real
posts.text:
Three ways to make a call to a parent about something real

When calls turn into a quick check, try one of these: ask about a project, ask them to teach you something, or share one small thing from your day.

Apply for the family beta at heykettle.com.
posts.alt: Three stacked comic panels. Dana walks down a leafy street on the phone asking, 'What are you working on this week?' Walt at his kitchen table with a chess set says, 'Come here, I will show you.' Dana on a park bench says, 'The bus driver sang today. Badly.' Captions: Ask about a project. Ask them to teach you. Share one small thing.

posts.title: A call can just be a call

script.say: My check-ins with my parents got tactical. How are you, how's work, okay, talk soon.
script.broll: Founder to camera, kitchen counter behind him.

script.say: I wasn't really calling to talk. I wanted to know their morning happened.
script.overlay: I wanted to know the morning happened

script.say: So I built Kettle. It notices that on the phone they already own, and tells us twice a day. If a morning is different, it asks them first.
script.overlay: Twice a day. Asks them first.
script.broll: Neutral b-roll: a plain phone face down on a kitchen table, no app visible.

script.say: Now a call can just be a call.

posts.text: People ask what Kettle knows about a parent. Three things: who, which routine, when. Not what they typed, who they called or where they went. What isn't collected can't leak.
posts.alt: Three-panel comic. Dana phones her dad: 'Okay if a note comes to me twice a day?' Walt, winding his wristwatch at his workbench, asks: 'Does it say anything else?' Dana, grinning, answers: 'Just that your morning happened.' Caption: He got a say.

posts.title: Their morning, my night

script.say: If your parents are a few time zones away, you know the problem.
You want to know how their day started, but your call lands in the middle of theirs, or in the middle of the night.
script.broll: Phone on a table, a mug beside it.

script.say: Kettle tells you twice a day that a normal morning happened, on the phone they already own. If a morning is different, it asks them first.

posts.text: A good call has no agenda. You just wanted to hear a voice. That is easier when you already know the morning was normal. For checking in, not checking up.
posts.alt: Three-panel comic. Dana walks through autumn leaves on the phone: 'No reason. Just wanted to hear you.' Walt on his porch with a chess set says: 'Good. I am losing to myself again.' Dana laughs. Caption: No agenda.
